faqs.q: Copperheads near Milton — how worried should a homeowner be?
faqs.a: Respectful, mostly about habits. Southern copperheads live in the Blackwater's hammock edges and leaf litter, are superbly camouflaged, and bite almost exclusively when stepped on or picked up. Boots and a flashlight in the bottomland, woodpiles away from the house, and a photo-from-distance rule for unknown snakes manage the risk well. A copperhead denning in a yard woodpile by the door is a legitimate specialist removal; the population in the forest is not a service item and never will be.

Milton.wildlife_intro:
Milton is Santa Rosa's county seat on the Blackwater River — a historic river town with brick downtown streets, surrounded by the Blackwater River State Forest, Yellow River marsh, and some of the finest paddling country in Florida. Forest-and-river wildlife dominates: raccoons and opossums in the historic homes, squirrels in the oak and pine canopy, armadillos in the yards, and along the river bottoms, the Panhandle's full snake cast including copperheads in the hammock litter and cottonmouths in the swamp.

Milton service is river-town service: historic-home craft downtown, acreage walks outside it, and snake identification done with Panhandle seriousness. The Blackwater's clear, sand-bottom creeks hold mostly harmless watersnakes and racers; the swamp tupelo bottoms hold the cottonmouths. We sort them by photo and habitat, remove what is lawful and resident, and leave the forest's population where it belongs — in the forest, which starts at the edge of nearly every Milton yard.

faqs.q: Our Navarre rental sits empty between military tenants — what is the risk?
faqs.a: The vacancy colony. Sound-side rentals that sit for a month in summer reliably host roof rats or raccoons by fall if any entry stands open — the Sound's vegetation feeds them and the quiet house shelters them. A turnover seal, documented with photos at each vacancy, converts that risk to near zero and gives owners and managers a dated record. It is the same lesson as every Florida rental market, with a military calendar attached: seal at vacancy, not after discovery.

faqs.q: Can you relocate a raccoon from my Gulf Breeze attic?
faqs.a: Only on Florida's strict conditions. Under FWC Rule 68A-9.010, a live-captured native animal must be released or handled within 24 hours, and an off-site release is lawful only within the same county, on 40 or more contiguous acres, with the release landowner's written permission — or it can be released on-site once the home is sealed. Raccoons are Florida's most-reported rabies carrier, so we never promise a casual drop-off in the woods, and nonnative animals such as iguanas and Muscovy ducks may never be relocated at all.

Gulf Breeze.wildlife_intro:
In Gulf Breeze, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — river and forest towns, Navarre beach suburbs, and Pace growth corridor — and features such as Blackwater River State Forest, East Bay, Santa Rosa Sound, Yellow River keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Gulf Breeze jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: What is digging the small sand mounds in my Jay yard?
faqs.a: That depends on the shape. Eastern moles leave raised surface tunnels and small molehills, armadillos leave scattered digging in beds and lawn edges, and in sandy north and central Florida soils a southeastern pocket gopher leaves a row of sand mounds. A large burrow with a wide, half-moon apron of sand is different — that is likely a gopher tortoise burrow, which is protected, carries a 25-foot permit buffer, and must be left alone. Call us and describe the digging and we will identify it before any work is planned.
